reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / GOLD & ATS guidelines
clinicalPearls: A multisystem granulomatous disorder of unknown cause in which the lungs and intrathoracic lymph nodes are most often involved
Presentations range from asymptomatic bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy found incidentally to cough, dyspnoea, and chest discomfort
Loefgren syndrome (bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, erythema nodosum, arthralgia, and fever) is an acute presentation with a favourable prognosis
Chest imaging is often staged by the presence of hilar adenopathy and parenchymal infiltration, with fibrosis in advanced disease
Diagnosis rests on compatible clinical and radiological features plus biopsy showing non-caseating granulomas, after exclusion of infection and other granulomatous disease
Serum ACE may be raised but is neither sensitive nor specific and should not be relied upon for diagnosis or monitoring
Hypercalcaemia and hypercalciuria can occur due to dysregulated vitamin D activation within granulomas
Many patients remit spontaneously; corticosteroids are reserved for significant or progressive organ involvement, with immunosuppressants as steroid-sparing options
reference.pathophysiology: Sarcoidosis is thought to arise when an unknown antigen triggers an exaggerated cell-mediated immune response in a genetically susceptible host. Antigen-presenting cells activate CD4 T-helper lymphocytes that secrete Th1 cytokines, driving accumulation of macrophages and their organisation into compact non-caseating epithelioid granulomas. In the lung these granulomas cluster along lymphatics and around bronchovascular structures. Granulomas may resolve or, with persistent inflammation, be replaced by fibrosis, causing irreversible architectural distortion and functional impairment.
additionalDifferentials: Berylliosis, which is clinically and histologically similar
additionalInvestigations: Chest radiography and CT to assess lymphadenopathy, parenchymal involvement, and fibrosis
Biopsy (often via endobronchial ultrasound-guided nodal sampling) to demonstrate non-caseating granulomas
Pulmonary function testing including diffusing capacity to gauge functional impairment
Serum and urinary calcium to detect dysregulated calcium metabolism
Assessment for extrapulmonary involvement including cardiac, ocular, hepatic, and neurological evaluation
redFlags: Symptoms or findings suggesting cardiac sarcoidosis such as arrhythmia, heart block, or heart failure
Neurosarcoidosis with cranial nerve or central nervous system involvement
Progressive pulmonary fibrosis or pulmonary hypertension
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is generally favourable, with a substantial proportion of patients undergoing spontaneous remission, especially in acute presentations such as Loefgren syndrome; however, chronic progressive disease with pulmonary fibrosis, cardiac involvement, or neurosarcoidosis carries greater morbidity and mortality.
pitfalls: Diagnosing sarcoidosis without excluding tuberculosis and other infective granulomatous disease
Relying on serum ACE levels for diagnosis or disease monitoring
Missing clinically silent but dangerous cardiac or neurological involvement
Treating asymptomatic or mildly affected patients who may remit without therapy
management: Observe asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic disease with serial monitoring, since spontaneous remission is common, particularly in Loefgren syndrome
Treat symptomatic or progressive pulmonary disease with oral corticosteroids as first-line therapy to suppress granulomatous inflammation
Add steroid-sparing immunosuppressants such as methotrexate or azathioprine for chronic disease or to limit corticosteroid toxicity
Reserve anti-TNF biologics such as infliximab for refractory or multi-organ disease
Manage acute Loefgren syndrome symptomatically with non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for arthralgia and erythema nodosum
Monitor lung function including diffusing capacity, and treat dysregulated calcium metabolism by avoiding excess vitamin D and sunlight
Screen actively for cardiac, ocular, hepatic, and neurological involvement and refer for specialist assessment when present
Consider pulmonary rehabilitation and referral for lung transplantation in end-stage pulmonary fibrosis
